section_text: This Act may be called the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. It extends to the whole of India. It applies to any person who is a Hindu by religion including Virashaiva, Lingayat, or follower of the Brahmo, Prarthana or Arya Samaj; any person who is a Buddhist, Jaina or Sikh by religion; and any person domiciled in the territories to whom this Act extends who is not a Muslim, Christian, Parsi or Jew by religion.

This Act applies to any person who is a Hindu by religion in any of its forms or developments including a Virashaiva, a Lingayat or a follower of the Brahmo, Prarthana or Arya Samaj.

This Act also applies to any person who is a Buddhist, Jaina or Sikh by religion.

This Act also applies to any other person domiciled in the territories to whom this Act extends who is not a Muslim, Christian, Parsi or Jew by religion, unless it is proved that any such person would not have been governed by the Hindu law or by any custom or usage as part of that law in respect of any of the matters dealt with herein if this Act had not been passed.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires:

(a) 'custom' and 'usage' signify any rule which, having been continuously and uniformly observed for a long time, has obtained the force of law among Hindus: Provided that the rule is certain and not unreasonable or opposed to public policy.

(b) 'district court' means, in any area for which there is a city civil court, that court, and in any other area, the principal civil court of original jurisdiction.

(c) 'full blood' and 'half blood' - two persons are said to be related to each other by full blood when they are descended from a common ancestor by the same wife, and by half blood when they are descended from a common ancestor but by different wives.

(d) 'uterine blood' - two persons are said to be related to each other by uterine blood when they are descended from a common ancestress but by different husbands.

(e) 'prescribed' means prescribed by rules made under this Act.

(f) Sapinda relationship: extends up to the fifth degree through the father and third degree through the mother.

A marriage may be solemnized between any two Hindus, if the following conditions are fulfilled, namely:

(i) Neither party has a spouse living at the time of the marriage. (Bigamy is an offence under Section 494/495 IPC / Section 82 BNS).

(ii) At the time of the marriage, neither party:
(a) is incapable of giving a valid consent to it in consequence of unsoundness of mind; or
(b) though capable of giving a valid consent, has been suffering from mental disorder of such a kind or to such an extent as to be unfit for marriage and the procreation of children; or
(c) has been subject to recurrent attacks of insanity.

(iii) The bridegroom has completed the age of twenty-one years and the bride the age of eighteen years at the time of the marriage.

(iv) The parties are not within the degrees of prohibited relationship unless the custom permits it.

(v) The parties are not sapindas of each other, unless the custom permits it.

Note: Marriage in contravention of conditions (i), (iv) or (v) is void. Contravention of condition (ii) makes the marriage voidable. Contravention of condition (iii) does not make the marriage void but is punishable.

A Hindu marriage may be solemnized in accordance with the customary rites and ceremonies of either party thereto.

Where such rites and ceremonies include the Saptapadi (that is, the taking of seven steps by the bridegroom and the bride jointly before the sacred fire), the marriage becomes complete and binding when the seventh step is taken.

Note: This section is important because it establishes that Hindu marriage is both a religious sacrament AND a legal act. Registration of marriage is not mandatory for validity but is recommended.

For the purpose of facilitating the proof of Hindu marriages, the State Government may make rules providing that the parties to any such marriage may have the particulars relating to their marriage entered in such manner and subject to such conditions as may be prescribed in a Hindu Marriage Register kept for the purpose.

Note: In the case of Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006), the Supreme Court directed all states to make registration of marriages compulsory for proof of marriage.

When either the husband or the wife has, without reasonable excuse, withdrawn from the society of the other, the aggrieved party may apply, by petition to the district court, for restitution of conjugal rights and the court, on being satisfied of the truth of the statements made in such petition and that there is no legal ground why the application should not be granted, may decree restitution of conjugal rights accordingly.

Explanation: The burden of proving 'reasonable excuse' shall be on the person who has withdrawn from the society.

Key Case: Saroj Rani v. Sudarshan Kumar (1984) SC upheld the constitutional validity of this section, viewing marriage as a social institution.

Either party to a marriage may present a petition praying for a decree of judicial separation on any of the grounds specified in section 13(1), and in the case of a wife also on any of the grounds specified in section 13(2).

Where a decree for judicial separation has been passed, it shall no longer be obligatory for the petitioner to cohabit with the respondent, but the court may rescind the decree if it considers it just and reasonable to do so.

Note: Judicial separation does not dissolve the marriage but suspends the duty of cohabitation.

Any marriage solemnized after the commencement of this Act shall be null and void if it contravenes any one of the conditions specified in clauses (i), (iv) and (v) of section 5 (Bigamy, Prohibited relationships, Sapinda relationships).

Note: A void marriage is void ab initio. Children born of such marriages are recognized as legitimate under Section 16.

Any marriage solemnized shall be voidable and may be annulled by a decree of nullity on any of the following grounds:
(a) Respondent's impotence preventing consummation.
(b) Contravention of Section 5(ii) (Unsoundness of mind).
(c) Consent obtained by force or fraud.
(d) Respondent was pregnant by someone else at the time of marriage.

Note: A voidable marriage is valid until annulled by a decree of court.

Any marriage may be dissolved by a decree of divorce on the ground that the other party:
(i) Committed voluntary sexual intercourse with another person (Adultery).
(ia) Treated the petitioner with Cruelty.
(ib) Deserted the petitioner for at least 2 years.
(ii) Converted to another religion.
(iii) Is of unsound mind or suffering from mental disorder.
(iv) Is suffering from a virulent and incurable form of leprosy.
(v) Is suffering from venereal disease in a communicable form.
(vi) Renounced the world by entering a religious order.
(vii) Not been heard of as being alive for 7 years.

(1A) Grounds for either party: (i) No resumption of cohabitation for 1 year after judicial separation; (ii) No restitution of conjugal rights for 1 year after decree.

In any proceeding under this Act, on a petition for dissolution of marriage by a decree of divorce, the court may, if it considers it just so to do having regard to the circumstances of the case, pass instead a decree for judicial separation.

A petition for dissolution of marriage may be presented to the district court by both the parties together on the ground that they have been living separately for a period of one year or more, that they have not been able to live together and that they have mutually agreed that the marriage should be dissolved.

Key Case: Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur (2017) SC held that the 6-month statutory waiting period is directory and not mandatory, and can be waived in exceptional circumstances.

section_title: No petition for divorce within one year of marriage
section_text:
Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, it shall not be competent for any court to entertain any petition for dissolution of a marriage by a decree of divorce, unless at the date of the presentation of the petition one year has elapsed since the date of the marriage.

Note: The court may allow earlier filing in cases of exceptional hardship to the petitioner or exceptional depravity on the part of the respondent.

section_title: Divorced persons when may marry again
section_text: When a marriage has been dissolved by a decree of divorce and either there is no right of appeal against the decree or, if there is such a right of appeal, the time for appealing has expired without an appeal having been presented, or an appeal has been presented but has been dismissed, it shall be lawful for either party to the marriage to marry again.

section_title: Legitimacy of children of void and voidable marriages
section_text:
Notwithstanding that a marriage is null and void under section 11, any child of such marriage shall be legitimate. Similarly, children of voidable marriages annulled under section 12 are also legitimate.

Note: Such children have the right to inherit the property of their parents but not the ancestral property of their parents' relatives (unless custom permits).

Any marriage between two Hindus solemnized after the commencement of this Act is void if at the date of such marriage either party had a husband or wife living; and the provisions of sections 494 and 495 of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860) shall apply accordingly (now Section 82 of BNS).

section_title: Punishment for contravention of conditions for Hindu marriage
section_text:
Every person who procures a marriage of himself or herself to be solemnized under this Act in contravention of conditions specified in:
(a) Section 5(iii) (Minority): Rigorous imprisonment up to 2 years or fine up to 1 lakh rupees, or both.
(b) Section 5(iv) or (v) (Prohibited/Sapinda relationship): Simple imprisonment up to 1 month or fine up to 1,000 rupees, or both.

section_title: Court to which petition shall be presented
section_text:
Every petition shall be presented to the district court within the local limits of whose ordinary original civil jurisdiction:
(i) the marriage was solemnized, or
(ii) the respondent resides at the time of presentation,
(iii) the parties to the marriage last resided together,
(iiia) in case the wife is the petitioner, where she is residing on the date of presentation, or
(iv) the petitioner is residing, in cases where respondent is outside India or not heard from for 7 years.

Every petition shall state as distinctly as the nature of the case admits the facts on which the claim to relief is founded and shall also state that there is no collusion between the petitioner and the other party to the marriage. The statements contained in every petition shall be verified by the petitioner in the manner required by law for the verification of plaints.

Subject to the other provisions contained in this Act and to such rules as the High Court may make, all proceedings under this Act shall be regulated, as far as may be, by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

section_title: Special provision relating to trial and disposal of petitions
section_text: The trial of a petition under this Act shall, so far as is practicable consistently with the interests of justice, be continued from day to day until its conclusion. Every petition shall be tried as expeditiously as possible and endeavor shall be made to conclude the trial within six months from the date of service of notice of the petition on the respondent.

section_title: Proceedings to be in camera and may not be published
section_text: Every proceeding under this Act shall be conducted in camera (in private), and it shall not be lawful for any person to print or publish any matter in relation to such proceeding except with the previous permission of the court. Contravention is punishable with fine up to 1,000 rupees.

In any proceeding under this Act, if the court is satisfied that any ground for granting relief exists and that the petitioner is not in any way taking advantage of his or her own wrong, the court shall decree such relief accordingly. Before granting relief, the court must make every endeavor to bring about a reconciliation between the parties.

section_title: Maintenance pendente lite and expenses of proceedings
section_text: Where either the wife or the husband has no independent income sufficient for support and the necessary expenses of the proceeding, the court may, on application, order the respondent to pay the monthly maintenance and expenses of the proceeding. Endeavor shall be made to dispose of the application within 60 days.

The court may, at the time of passing any decree or later, order the respondent to pay to the applicant for her or his maintenance and support such gross sum or such monthly or periodical sum for a term not exceeding the life of the applicant, having regard to the respondent's income and other property, and the conduct of the parties.

In any proceeding under this Act, the court may, from time to time, pass such interim orders and make such provisions in the decree as it may deem just and proper with respect to the custody, maintenance, and education of minor children, consistently with their wishes wherever possible.

In any proceeding under this Act, the court may make such provisions in the decree as it deems just and proper with respect to any property presented, at or about the time of marriage, which may belong jointly to both the husband and the wife.

All decrees made by the court in any proceeding under this Act shall be appealable as decrees of the court. Every such appeal shall be preferred within a period of 90 days from the date of the decree or order.

Note: In matrimonial cases, the 90-day period is critical for determining when a person can marry again under Section 15.
This Act may be called the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. It extends to the whole of India. It codifies the law relating to intestate succession among Hindus (including Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs).

Save as otherwise expressly provided in this Act, any text, rule or interpretation of Hindu law or any custom or usage as part of that law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to have effect with respect to any matter for which provision is made in this Act.

section_title: Devolution of interest in coparcenary property
section_text:
On and from the commencement of the amendment in 2005, in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener shall by birth become a coparcener in her own right in the same manner as the son. She has the same rights and liabilities as a son.

Key Case: Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) SC: The 2005 amendment is retrospective. Daughters have coparcenary rights by birth, irrespective of whether the father was alive on the date of amendment or not.

section_title: General rules of succession in the case of males
Distribution of property among heirs in Class I
section_text:
Property is divided among Class I heirs as follows:
- Widow(s) together take one share.
- Surviving sons, daughters, and the mother each take one share.
- Heirs in the branch of each pre-deceased son or daughter take together one share.

section_title: Property of a female Hindu to be her absolute property
section_text:
Any property possessed by a female Hindu, whether acquired before or after the commencement of this Act, shall be held by her as full owner thereof and not as a limited owner.

Key Case: V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy (1977) SC: Abolished the old concept of 'limited estate' for Hindu women, making them absolute owners of inherited property.

section_title: General rules of succession in case of female Hindus
Full blood preferred to half blood
section_text: Heirs related to an intestate by full blood shall be preferred to heirs related by half blood, if the nature of the relationship is the same in every other respect.

A child who was in the womb at the time of the death of an intestate and who is subsequently born alive shall have the same right to inherit to the intestate as if he or she had been born before the death of the intestate.

section_title: Certain widows remarrying may not inherit as widows (REPEALED)
section_text: Note: This section (which barred certain widows from inheriting if they remarried) has been repealed by the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 in several contexts, though some restrictions remain under specific custom.

A person who commits murder or abets the commission of murder shall be disqualified from inheriting the property of the person murdered, or any other property in furtherance of the succession to which he or she committed or abetted the commission of the murder.

Where, before or after the commencement of this Act, a Hindu has ceased or ceases to be a Hindu by conversion to another religion, children born to him or her after such conversion and their descendants shall be disqualified from inheriting the property of any of their Hindu relatives, unless such children or descendants are Hindus at the time when the succession opens.

Any Hindu may dispose of by will or other testamentary disposition any property, which is capable of being so disposed of by him or by her, in accordance with the provisions of the Indian Succession Act, 1925.
Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956. Extends to the whole of India. Applies to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, and Sikhs.

(a) 'minor' means a person who has not completed the age of eighteen years;
(b) 'guardian' means a person having the care of the person of a minor or of his property or of both.

section_title: Natural guardians of a Hindu minor
section_text:
The natural guardian of a Hindu minor, in respect of the minor's person as well as property, are:
(a) in case of a boy/unmarried girl: Father, and after him, the Mother. Proviso: Custody of a minor under 5 years shall ordinarily be with the mother.
(b) illegitimate child: Mother, and after her, the Father.

Key Case: Githa Hariharan v. RBI(1999) SC: 'After' the father does not mean just after death, but includes situations where father is absent/unable to act.

section_title: Welfare of minor to be paramount consideration
section_text: In the appointment or declaration of any person as guardian, the welfare of the minor shall be the paramount consideration. No person shall be entitled to the guardianship by virtue of the provisions of this Act if the court is of opinion that it will not be for the welfare of the minor.
Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956. Extends to the whole of India.
No adoption is valid unless: (i) Person adopting has capacity and right; (ii) Person giving in adoption has capacity; (iii) Person adopted is capable; (iv) Conditions in Section 11 are met.

section_title: Capacity of male Hindu to adopt
section_text: Any male Hindu of sound mind and not a minor can adopt a son/daughter. If he has a wife living, he shall not adopt except with her consent (unless she renounced the world or is of unsound mind).

section_title: Capacity of female Hindu to adopt
section_text: Any female Hindu of sound mind and not a minor can adopt a son/daughter if she is unmarried, widowed, or divorced.

A Hindu wife is entitled to be maintained by her husband during her lifetime. She can live separately without forfeiting maintenance if he is guilty of desertion, cruelty, leprosy, or keeps a concubine.

section_title: Maintenance of children and aged parents
section_text: A Hindu is bound to maintain his or her minor children (legitimate or illegitimate) and his or her aged or infirm parents.
